content: The term peptic is an adjective used to describe any part of the body that typically has an acidic lumen. It is a term commonly used in medical and veterinary contexts, particularly in reference to humans. Under normal conditions, the peptic regions of the human body include the stomach and the duodenum. In individuals with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), the esophagus—especially its lower portion—may also become acidic. Additionally, in cases of Meckel's diverticulum, the diverticulum may contain acid-producing cells, which can predispose the individual to peptic ulcers or even perforation. In individuals with altered anatomy, such as those who have undergone a gastrectomy or an esophagectomy with ileal transplantation to replace the esophagus, acidity may occur in regions of the body that are not typically acidic. However, in normal human anatomy and in the vast majority of individuals, the gastrointestinal tract is the only part of the body that is considered peptic. One of the most common issues affecting peptic regions is the development of peptic ulcers. These ulcers are primarily caused by bacterial infections, rather than the acidic environment itself.
